Title: A novel transcendental metaphor metaheuristic algorithm based on power method
Text:
A novel transcendental metaphor 
metaheuristic algorithm based on 
power method
Huiying Zhang1,2, Hanshuo Wu1,2, Yifei Gong1,2, Xiao Pan1,2 & Qipeng Zhong1,2
This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm-the Power Method Algorithm (PMA), which 
is inspired by the power iteration method to solve complex optimization problems. PMA simulates 
the process of computing dominant eigenvalues and eigenvectors, incorporating strategies such as 
stochastic angle generation and adjustment factors, effectively addressing eigenvalue problems in 
large sparse matrices. The algorithm is rigorously evaluated on 49 benchmark functions from the CEC 
2017 and CEC 2022 test suites. Quantitative analysis reveals that PMA surpasses nine state-of-the-
art metaheuristic algorithms and performs better, with average Friedman rankings of 3, 2.71, and 
2.69 for 30, 50, and 100 dimensions, respectively. Statistical tests including the Wilcoxon rank-sum 
and Friedman test further confirm the robustness and reliability. Additionally, PMA demonstrates 
exceptional performance in solving eight real-world engineering optimization problems, consistently 
delivering optimal solutions. Experimental results show that PMA achieves an effective balance 
between exploration and exploitation, effectively avoiding local optima while maintaining high 
convergence efficiency. Therefore, PMA demonstrates notable competitiveness and practical value in 
interdisciplinary complex optimization tasks.

Numerous engineering problems1 such as mechanical path planning problems2 production scheduling 
problems3 economic dispatch problems4 resource allocation problems5 and other issues encountered in real 
life can be viewed as optimization problems. The increasing engineering demands have rendered optimization 
problems more complex with the development of society and advancements in technology. To better address 
these optimization challenges, numerous optimization strategies have been proposed., These optimization 
strategies can be categorized into two main groups based on their applicability: deterministic methods6 and 
stochastic methods7.
Deterministic methods are designed based on mathematical theories and the structural characteristics of 
problems, such as Newton’s method, linear programming and gradient descent8. These methods effectively solve 
specific problems under strict assumptions and can guarantee consistency and high precision in results, which 
makes them suitable for high-accuracy applications9,10. However, these methods are limited by their stringent 
requirements on problem structure, susceptibility to local optima, and high computational complexity.
Stochastic methods, especially heuristic and metaheuristic algorithms, effectively address complex 
optimization problems by incorporating random factors and diverse search strategies. Compared to deterministic 
methods, the performance of heuristic algorithms is influenced by the problem structure and characteristics. 
They solve problems quickly, but the obtained solutions are usually only near-optimal. Deterministic methods 
can achieve optimal solutions but require substantial time for large-scale problems. The limitation of heuristic 
algorithms lies in their reliance on heuristic rules to guide local search processes, which generate different 
solutions based on varying initial points. Consequently, the quality of the solutions may be unstable and prone 
to converging to local optima11.
In recent years, metaheuristic algorithms have garnered significant attention and demonstrated their 
effectiveness in engineering optimization problems, such as engineering design, path planning, production 
scheduling, resource allocation, and parameter optimization problems. Metaheuristic algorithms explore 
the solution space by simulating certain phenomena and behaviors in nature or some theories, remaining 
independent of problem structures. Through incorporating random factors and diverse search strategies, the 
extensive exploration is achieved in the solution space. Updating the solution in each iteration and comparing

grounded in the Newton-Raphson method; Stadium Spectators Optimization (SSO) algorithm14 which inspired 
by the influence of spectator behavior on players; Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm (SBOA)15 which 
draws inspiration from the survival behaviors of secretary birds in their natural habitat; Tornado Optimization 
Algorithm(TOC)16 which simulates the natural processes of tornadoes; and the Neural Population Dynamics 
Optimization Algorithm(NPDOA)17 which models the dynamics of neural populations during cognitive 
activities. Despite their promising performance, they still face challenges such as achieving a balance between 
global exploration and local exploitation, managing the trade-off between convergence speed and accuracy, 
dependency on initial solutions, and adaptability to complex problems. These issues represent common 
challenges encountered by many metaheuristic algorithms.
The No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem18 proposed by Wolpert and Macready indicates that if an algorithm 
performs well on some problems, it must perform poorly on others. There is no algorithm that performs best in 
all situations, nor is there a universal metaheuristic algorithm that consistently outperforms other algorithms 
across optimization problems. This observation underscores the necessity of proposing new metaheuristic 
algorithms and improving existing ones.
The power method iteration is highly effective for solving the dominant eigenvalue and its corresponding 
eigenvector of a matrix, which leads us to ponder whether we can uncover deeper potential value in the power 
method iteration and extend its application to a broader range of optimization problems. Guided by this idea, 
through extensive research and experimentation, a novel algorithm—the PMA algorithm is proposed. This 
algorithm is based on the power method iteration, and breaks through traditional application boundaries 
by innovatively integrating it into the optimization solving process, thereby providing new perspectives and 
methodologies for addressing a series of complex problems. The innovative aspects of PMA are primarily 
reflected in the following areas:
	1.	 Integration of the power method with random perturbations. During the exploration phase, the power 
method with random perturbations is innovatively introduced into the vector update process. Combined 
with a random step, the optimization process of the PMA algorithm is simulated. Based on the tendency of 
the power method for local search, the step size is fine-tuned, and the current solution’s gradient information 
is used to ensure the local search accuracy while maintaining a balance with global search capabilities. This 
approach offers potential improvements for optimization problems solved using gradient-based or linear 
update methods.
	2.	 Application of random geometric transformations. During the development phase, a randomness and non­
linear transformation mechanism is established, and integrates random geometric transformations and 
computational adjustment factor strategies to update candidate positions, thereby the search diversity and 
exploration capabilities are enhanced. This approach emphasizes global search to expand the solution space.
	3.	 Balanced strategy for exploration and exploitation. The algorithm synergistically combines the local ex­
ploitation characteristics of the power method with the global exploration features of random geometric 
transformations, and an effective balance between exploration and exploitation is achieved. It not only utiliz­
es current optimal information for fine local searches but also conducts global exploration through random 
jumps. Compared to traditional algorithms, it demonstrates advantages in global search capability and con­
vergence efficiency.
	4.	 Integration of mathematical theory with metaheuristic algorithms. Using the characteristic of the power 
method, which gradually approximates the principal eigenvector during computing the principal eigenvalue 
of a matrix, and the gradient information of the current solution is effectively utilized during local search. By 
simulating the core operations of the power method, the sequence of position vectors converges toward the 
principal eigenvector during the iterations, providing a solid mathematical foundation for local search, and 
the precision of the local search is enhanced. Furthermore, the algorithm possesses stronger generalization 
capabilities and adaptability, making it suitable for optimization problems across various fields.
The main contributions of this study can be summarized as follows:
•	 The PMA algorithm is a novel metaheuristic algorithm based on the power method theory, with its math­
ematical principles derived from the process of solving for the dominant eigenvalue and its corresponding 
eigenvector using the power method, and it incorporates mathematical strategies such as stochastic angles 
and computational adjustment factors into the power method framework.
•	 The performance of the PMA algorithm is evaluated using the CEC2017 and CEC2022 benchmark suites. 
The experimental results demonstrate that the PMA algorithm outperforms other comparative algorithms, 
proving its effectiveness and reliability in solving various complex optimization problems.
•	 The experiments and analyses on the PMA algorithm are conducted in terms of convergence speed, accuracy, 
stability, and robustness, demonstrating its exceptional performance.
•	 Successfully solving eight engineering design problems that demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the 
PMA algorithm.

Related work
Compared to deterministic methods and heuristic algorithms, metaheuristic algorithms have emerged as the 
preferred choice and demonstrated significant advantages in solving numerous optimization problems. It is 
classified into five categories based on the different inspirations of metaheuristic algorithms, as shown in Fig. 1: 
evolution-based algorithms, human behavior-based algorithms, swarm intelligence algorithms, mathematics-
based algorithms, and physics-based algorithms. A detailed review is provided in the following subsections.
Evolution-based algorithms
Evolutionary algorithms generally draw techniques and inspiration from biological systems, such as inheritance, 
mutation, selection, recombination, and reproduction. Genetic algorithm holds a significant position among 
evolutionary algorithms. It simulates the process through which organisms in nature evolve via inheritance, 
mutation, and natural selection. The solutions to problems are encoded as chromosomes, and new solutions are 
generated through genetic operations. Solutions with high fitness are selected to proceed to the next generation. 
Through multiple generations of evolution, the algorithm gradually approximates the optimal solution to the 
problem. While genetic algorithm19 performs well in addressing some challenging issues, it also suffers from 
limitations such as inadequate local search capabilities and a tendency to converge too early. The performance 
of genetic algorithms is influenced by factors such as the complexity of the fitness function, parameters of 
genetic operations, and the balance between population size and number of iterations. Common evolutionary 
algorithms are listed in Table 1.
Human behavior-based algorithms
Humans can devise numerous corresponding solutions and strategies when faced with challenging problems. 
Therefore, inspiration can be found in human problem-solving approaches and social behaviors. As the recently 
proposed Hiking Optimization Algorithm, its exploration process simulates the way hikers select paths in 
different terrains. In terms of adaptive adjustment, hikers adjust their steps and routes based on the terrain and 
physical condition. Other common algorithms based on human behavior are listed in Table 2.
Swarm intelligence algorithms
Swarm intelligence algorithms are a class of optimization algorithms designed inspired by the collective 
behavior of biological swarms in nature. It solves complex optimization problems by simulating the collaborative 
behaviors of biological swarms, such as bird flocking and ant foraging. In such algorithms, a swarm composed 
of multiple individuals conducts a search within the problem’s solution space. Each individual represents a 
potential solution to the problem, and through information exchange and collaboration among individuals, they 
adjust themselves to gradually approach the optimal solution to the problem. Swarm intelligence algorithms 
typically exhibit characteristics such as decentralization, self-organization, adaptability, and parallelism. Other 
swarm intelligence algorithms are listed in Table 3.

Mathematics-based algorithms
Mathematics encompasses numerous branches, such as number theory, algebra, geometry, calculus, probability 
theory, statistics, and so on. Some researchers have introduced mathematical concepts or models to propose 
algorithms, providing unique perspectives and methods for solving complex problems. These algorithms break 
through the conventional thinking patterns of traditional optimization algorithms and open up new avenues for 
optimization. Other mathematics-based algorithms are listed in Table 4.
Physics-based algorithms
Researchers draw inspiration from certain physical principles or phenomena to bring novel ideas and methods for 
solving complex problems. For instance, Simulated Annealing (SA) is a physics-based metaheuristic algorithm. 
It is inspired by the annealing process of solids and accepts worsening solutions with a certain probability to 
avoid getting stuck in local optima. Another example is the Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSA), which is 
inspired by Newton’s law of universal gravitation. In this algorithm, each individual is considered as an object 
with mass, and individuals interact with each other through gravitational forces. Individuals with larger masses 
exert greater attractive forces on others, guiding the search direction. Other physics-based algorithms are listed 
in Table 5.

Heuristic algorithm beyond metaphor
Many metaheuristic algorithms are constructed based on metaphors. For example, genetic algorithms 
metaphorically represent the biological evolution process, including crossover, mutation, and selection of genes; 
particle swarm optimization metaphorically represents the foraging behavior of bird flocks. These metaphors 
assist in understanding the fundamental principles and operational modes of the algorithms.
Going beyond metaphors implies that metaheuristic algorithms no longer solely rely on intuitive phenomena 
from nature or society for their design and understanding. Instead, they approach the problem from more 
abstract perspectives, such as mathematics and computational theory. It pursues a more general optimization 
framework, not constrained by the operational modes dictated by any specific metaphor. Such algorithms 
can more flexibly adapt to various types of optimization problems and dynamically adjust the search strategy 
according to the characteristics of the problem. Metaheuristic algorithms beyond metaphors may integrate 
multiple diverse concepts or techniques, rather than relying on a single metaphorical source, such as different 
branches of mathematics, to construct more powerful optimization tools. A metaheuristic algorithm beyond 
metaphors is proposed in this study, developed based on the power method.
Algorithmic challenges
In recent years, numerous novel metaheuristic algorithms have been proposed, which exhibit promising 
performance. However, they still exhibit certain limitations.
	1.	 The Newton-Raphson-Based Optimization (NRBO) algorithm initially randomly initializes the population, 
then precisely explores feasible regions using the Newton-Raphson Search Rule (NRSR) to accelerate conver­
gence. Meanwhile, the Trap Avoidance Operation (TAO) combines the best position and the current vector 
position to generate high-quality solutions, avoiding local optima. It is characterized by strong evolutionary 
capability, fast search speed, powerful optimization ability, and high balance between exploration and ex­
ploitation.
	2.	 The Stadium Spectators Optimization (SSO) algorithm simulates the interaction between spectators and 
players in a stadium, treating spectator behaviors as search agents. It searches by moving toward the best 
individual, random individuals, and random vectors between search agents. The algorithm balances explora­
tion and exploitation phases through parameter balancing and is characterized by its parameter-free nature 
and robust performance.
	3.	 The Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm (SBOA) simulates secretary birds hunting snakes to design the 
exploration phase, utilizing differential evolution strategies, Brownian motion, individual historical best 
positions, and Lévy flight strategies for searching. Meanwhile, it mimics the exploitation phase of escap­
ing predators to achieve a balance between exploration and exploitation. This algorithm is characterized by 
strong global search capability, fast convergence speed, good robustness, and minimal parameters.
	4.	 The Tornado optimizer with Coriolis Artificial force (TOC) based on the formation and development of tor­
nadoes. This algorithm exploits the dynamic characteristics of tornadoes and inter-individual information 
exchange mechanisms to rapidly locate promising regions within the search space and quickly converge to 
near-optimal solutions.
	5.	 The Neural Population Dynamics Optimization Algorithm (NPDOA) derives from the population theory 
in theoretical neuroscience. Its dynamical characteristics of neuronal populations during cognitive activ­
ities and constructs the algorithm based on trajectory variations in neural state space. The algorithm em­
ploys multiple strategies, such as the attractor trend strategy, coupled perturbation strategy, and information 
projection strategy. The combination of these strategies effectively balances exploration and exploitation, 
demonstrating strong adaptability to various optimization problems.
Despite their excellent performance on specific problems, these algorithms have the following limitations: The 
NRBO algorithm is highly sensitive to initial value selection, which affects its convergence and results. SSO 
algorithm lacks a robust theoretical foundation and performs inadequately in high-dimensional problems, 
exhibiting moderate stability in results. SBOA has limited local search precision and difficulties in handling 
complex constraints. TOC tends to prematurely converge, and the search efficiency is reduced in later 
optimization stages. NPDOA faces challenges in parameter tuning and requires further theoretical validation. 
In summary, contemporary metaheuristic algorithms face the following challenges:
•	 Premature Convergence: The algorithm becomes trapped in a local optimum prematurely during the search 
process, failing to effectively explore the global solution space.
•	 Parameter Sensitivity: Algorithm performance is highly dependent on parameter settings, which are complex 
to tune and lack generalizability.
•	 Lack of Theoretical Analysis: The lack of rigorous mathematical foundations and theoretical underpinnings 
hinders systematic interpretation of their performance characteristics and operational behavior.
•	 Exploration - Exploitation Trade-off: It is inherently challenging to establish an effective equilibrium between 
global search (exploration) and local optimization (exploitation) during the iterative optimization process.
•	 Adaptability Issues: Limited adaptability to heterogeneous optimization environments results in unstable per­
formance across different problem types or search spaces, indicating insufficient generalizability.

Results and discussion
Selection of test functions
To evaluate the performance of this algorithm, the CEC201760 and CEC202261 benchmark function sets are 
chosen. The CEC2017 set comprises a total of 29 benchmark functions. Among them, F1 to F5 are unimodal 
functions (with F2 officially removed), F6 to F9 are multimodal functions, F10 to F19 are hybrid functions, 
and F20 to F30 are composite functions. The CEC2022 set comprises 12 single-objective test functions with 
boundary constraints. Among them, Functions F1 and F2 are unimodal functions, F3 to F6 are multimodal 
functions, F7 and F8 are hybrid functions, and F9 to F12 are composite functions. These test functions are 
diverse and complex, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm’s effectiveness.
Competitive study of the new algorithm
Using the CEC 2017 benchmark function set, the PMA algorithm is compared with nine well-known and high-
performing algorithms to verify its accuracy. These include the Golden Jackal Optimization (GJO)62 Harris 
Hawks Optimization (HHO)63 Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO)64 Newton-Raphson-Based Optimization 
(NRBO)13 Stochastic Cuckoo Search Algorithm (NOA)65 Sine Cosine Algorithm (SCA)66 Subtractive Average-
Based Optimizer (SABO)67 Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA)68 and Arithmetic Optimization Algorithm 
(AOA)50. The comparison is made across various dimensions to test the accuracy of the PMA algorithm. 
Furthermore, the PMA algorithm is also tested against nine other algorithms that have shown good performance 
in solving optimization problems using the CEC 2022 benchmark function set, namely the Attraction-Repulsion 
Optimization Algorithm (AROA)69 GPSOGSA70 Fire Hawk Optimization (FHO)71 Moth Flame Optimization 
(MFO)72 Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)73 Simple Genetic Algorithm (SGA)74 PID Search Algorithm 
(PSA)75 Love Evolutionary Algorithm (LEA)25 and Bacterial Whale Optimization (BWO)76. This is done to 
demonstrate the advantages of the PMA algorithm. To ensure the fairness of the experiments, the population 
size is uniformly set to N = 30 and the maximum number of iterations is set to T = 500 for all tests, and each 
algorithm is run 30 times independently for each test function to obtain average values, standard deviations, 
and other relevant data. The mean and standard deviation are used to measure the average convergence and 
robustness of the algorithms. The comprehensive performance of each algorithm is ranked using the Friedman 
ranking to reflect its overall capability. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test (or Rank-Sum test) can be employed to 
determine whether there are significant differences between the PMA algorithm and other algorithms. The null

Computational complexity analysis
This study employs Big O notation to rigorously analyze the runtime complexity of the PMA (Power Method 
Algorithm). System Specifications for Optimization Process: CUP: CORE i9. Frequency: 2.2  GHz. RAM: 
32 GB. Hard drive: 2 TB. The algorithm can be decomposed into three primary components: initialization, 
position update, and fitness evaluation. The computational complexity of each component is quantified 
as follows: Initialization: O(N), Position Update: O(T⋅N⋅(N + dim)), Fitness Evaluation: O(T⋅N), where 
N, dim, and T denote the population size, problem dimensionality, and maximum iterations, respectively. 
Thus, the total computational complexity of PMA is formulated as: O(PMA) = O(Initialization) + O(Position 
Update) + O(Fitness Evaluation) = O(N) + O(T⋅N⋅(N + dim)) + O(T⋅N). To further investigate the computational 
complexity of the PMA algorithm, Table 15 presents the measured execution times of PMA and comparative 
algorithms on selected composite functions from the CEC 2017 50-dimensional test suite.

Discussion
The PMA proposed in this study demonstrates exceptional performance, particularly in addressing complex, 
high-dimensional, and multimodal optimization problems. Inspired by the power iteration method—a classical 
mathematical technique for computing dominant eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices—PMA achieves a 
unique balance between exploration and exploitation by integrating this traditional mathematical approach with 
stochastic perturbations and random geometric transformations. This balance is a critical challenge in the design 
of metaheuristic algorithms.
Innovative integration of power method with stochastic perturbations
One of the most significant innovations of PMA lies in its integration of the power method with stochastic 
perturbations during the exploration phase, employing multi-layer power iterations to compute dominant 
eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Traditional power iteration methods are deterministic and prone to converging to 
local optima, especially in high-dimensional spaces. Through random step sizes and perturbations introduced in 
the search space, which effectively avoids premature convergence and escaping local optima, and the issues faced 
by metaheuristic algorithms are solved. The random perturbations are generated using a normal distribution, 
introducing a controlled level of randomness into the vector update process. This approach not only preserves the 
local search capabilities of the power method but also enhances the global exploration potential. An exceptional

Random geometric transformations for enhanced exploitation
During the exploitation phase, random geometric transformations (such as random angles and adjustment 
factors) are used to dynamically adjust the search direction and step size, which significantly enhances the search 
efficiency and convergence stability of PMA in high - dimensional and multimodal problems. Introducing 
nonlinear changes that enable PMA to explore the solution space more thoroughly and effectively avoid local 
optima, especially excelling in high-dimensional complex problems.
Balance between exploration and exploitation
An exceptional balance between exploration and exploitation is achieved by integrating the local search 
capabilities of the power method with the global exploration potential of stochastic strategies, which is a critical 
challenge in metaheuristic algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that the PMA exhibits outstanding 
performance in benchmark tests, particularly in high-dimensional problems (50 and 100 dimensions), 
significantly outperforming other state-of-the-art algorithms.
Robustness and stability
The robustness and stability of PMA have been validated through statistical tests such as the Wilcoxon rank-sum 
test and the Friedman test. The algorithm’s solution distributions are more concentrated with fewer outliers, 
demonstrating its high stability.
Application to real-world engineering problems
PMA demonstrates exceptional performance in multiple real-world engineering optimization problems, 
such as spring design and pressure vessel design, consistently proposing optimal solutions. Therefore, PMA 
demonstrates superior capability in handling complex constraints and nonlinear problems.
In conclusion, PMA provides a novel and effective approach to solving complex optimization problems. 
The scalability, robustness, and stability of PMA make it a powerful tool for high-dimensional and multimodal 
optimization challenges.
